note: Missions that failed, were cancelled, ended early, or cost lives. when is the date of the loss or decision (year only where the day is not well defined). kind: crew (lives lost), lost (spacecraft lost), ended (ended before its time), cancelled (never flew). primary names the official record; more links to a longer account. Soviet-era casualty figures are disputed and given as ranges.

missions.for: The first test launch of the R-16, a new intercontinental missile, at Baikonur.
missions.far: Fully fuelled on the pad, half an hour from launch, with dozens of engineers still working around it to meet a deadline.
missions.what: A stray electrical signal ignited the second-stage engine while the rocket stood on the pad. It burned through the stage below and the whole vehicle exploded. Marshal Mitrofan Nedelin, who commanded the programme and had been sitting beside the rocket, was among the dead. The official toll, released decades later, is 78; other estimates run well above 100. The Soviet Union kept it secret until 1989.
missions.primary: Soviet state commission findings, declassified from 1989

missions.for: The first crewed flight of the Apollo spacecraft, in Earth orbit.
missions.far: A launch rehearsal on the pad, three weeks before flight.
missions.what: A spark, probably from damaged wiring, started a fire in a cabin filled with pure oxygen at higher than atmospheric pressure. The hatch opened inward and could not be forced against the pressure. Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died within a minute. The spacecraft was redesigned with a quick-opening hatch, fireproof materials and a mixed-gas atmosphere on the pad; twenty months later Apollo 7 flew.
missions.primary: Report of the Apollo 204 Review Board, 1967

missions.for: The first crewed flight of the Soyuz spacecraft, meant to dock with a second Soyuz.
missions.far: A day in orbit. One solar panel never unfolded, leaving the craft short of power and hard to steer; the second launch was called off.
missions.what: Vladimir Komarov brought the crippled ship through re-entry by hand. Then the main parachute stayed jammed in its container and the reserve tangled in the drogue. The capsule hit the ground at about 140 km/h. He was the first person to die during a spaceflight.

missions.for: The first crew to live aboard a space station, Salyut 1.
missions.far: Twenty-three days on the station, a record at the time, and a normal undocking.
missions.what: When the descent capsule separated, the jolt shook open a breathing valve 168 km up. The cabin lost its air in under two minutes. The crew wore no pressure suits because three men in suits did not fit. Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev were found dead in their seats after a flawless automatic landing. They remain the only people to have died in space itself.

missions.for: The 25th Space Shuttle flight, carrying a communications satellite and Christa McAuliffe, who was to teach lessons from orbit.
missions.far: 73 seconds.
missions.what: A rubber O-ring sealing a joint in the right-hand booster had stiffened in the overnight frost and failed to seal. Flame escaped, burned into the external tank and the vehicle broke apart. Engineers had warned the night before against launching in the cold. Lost: Dick Scobee, Michael Smith, Judith Resnik, Ellison Onizuka, Ronald McNair, Gregory Jarvis and Christa McAuliffe.
missions.primary: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission), 1986

missions.for: Sixteen days of science experiments in orbit.
missions.far: The whole mission. Sixteen minutes from landing.
missions.what: 82 seconds after launch a piece of insulating foam the size of a briefcase broke off the fuel tank and struck the left wing, punching a hole in its heat shield. Nobody knew how bad it was. On re-entry, hot gas entered the wing and the orbiter came apart over Texas. Lost: Rick Husband, William McCool, Michael Anderson, David Brown, Kalpana Chawla, Laurel Clark and Ilan Ramon.

missions.for: Three more Moon landings, with longer stays and more ambitious sites, among them the crater Copernicus and possibly Tycho.
missions.far: The rockets and most of the spacecraft were built. Crews were in training.
missions.what: Apollo 20 was cancelled in January 1970 so its Saturn V could launch the Skylab space station. Apollos 18 and 19 followed that September, cut for budget reasons after public interest faded and Apollo 13 nearly killed its crew. Two of the unused Saturn V rockets now lie on their sides as museum exhibits in Houston and Florida.
missions.primary: NASA budget announcements, January and September 1970

missions.for: The first landings on Mars, each with a small tethered rover on skis.
missions.far: Mars 2's lander crashed on 27 November 1971, the first human-made object to reach the surface. Mars 3 made the first soft landing five days later.
missions.what: Mars 3 began transmitting a picture 90 seconds after touchdown and fell silent less than 20 seconds later, having sent a grey, featureless partial frame. It had landed in the middle of a planet-wide dust storm. The cause was never established.
missions.primary: Soviet Academy of Sciences mission reports

missions.for: Landing a cosmonaut on the Moon before the United States.
missions.far: Four launches of the 105-metre N1 between 1969 and 1972. None survived its first stage.
missions.what: The first stage clustered 30 engines, and there was no stand large enough to test them firing together, so each flight was the test. The second attempt, on 3 July 1969, fell back and destroyed its launch pad in one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded. Its chief designer, Sergei Korolev, had died in 1966. The programme was suspended in 1974 and its existence denied until 1989.

missions.for: A reusable spaceplane to match the American Shuttle.
missions.far: One flight, on 15 November 1988: two orbits with nobody aboard and a fully automatic runway landing in a crosswind, which the Shuttle never did.
missions.what: The Soviet Union dissolved three years later and the money went with it. The programme was formally ended in 1993. In May 2002 the roof of its hangar at Baikonur collapsed, destroying the only Buran that had flown and killing eight workers.

missions.for: A year of mapping Mars from orbit: the first American mission there since Viking, seventeen years earlier.
missions.far: Eleven months and 720 million km, to three days short of arrival.
missions.what: Contact stopped while the spacecraft was pressurising its fuel tanks for the braking burn, and never resumed. The inquiry's best explanation is that oxidiser had seeped past valves during the long cruise, met fuel in the plumbing and ruptured a line, sending the craft into a spin.
missions.primary: Mars Observer Mission Failure Investigation Board report, 1993

missions.for: An orbiter, two landers and two ground penetrators, with instruments from more than twenty countries. At six tonnes it was the heaviest interplanetary probe yet launched.
missions.far: Earth orbit.
missions.what: The rocket's fourth stage failed to fire a second time, and the probe fell back into the atmosphere within a day, coming down somewhere over the Pacific, Chile or Bolivia. Russia did not launch another planetary mission for fifteen years.

missions.for: Studying Martian weather and relaying signals for a lander due ten weeks later.
missions.far: All the way to Mars.
missions.what: Software on the ground reported thruster firings in pound-force seconds. The navigation team's software expected newton-seconds, a factor of 4.45 different. Over nine months the error pushed the trajectory low. The orbiter passed about 57 km above the surface, where 80 km was the least it could survive, and burned up or skipped back into space.
missions.primary: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I report, 1999

missions.for: Digging for water ice near the Martian south pole. It also carried two small probes meant to slam into the ground and bury themselves.
missions.far: Atmospheric entry. Nothing was heard after that.
missions.what: The most likely cause: when the landing legs snapped open, the jolt was read by the software as touchdown, and the engine was shut off about 40 metres above the ground. The fault had shown up in testing and been misread. Both penetrator probes were lost too. Its design was reflown as Phoenix, which landed safely in 2008 and found the ice.
missions.primary: Report on the Loss of the Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 Missions, JPL, 2000

missions.for: Close flybys of at least two comets, to compare their nuclei.
missions.far: Six weeks in Earth orbit after launch.
missions.what: It fired its solid rocket motor to leave for deep space while out of radio contact, as planned, and never called back. Telescopes found three pieces where one spacecraft should have been. The inquiry concluded that the motor's exhaust probably overheated the body of the craft.

missions.for: Japan's first mission to another planet: studying how the solar wind strips the Martian atmosphere.
missions.far: Five and a half years in space and a pass 1,000 km above Mars.
missions.what: A valve fault in 1998 cost fuel and forced a four-year detour. In 2002 a solar flare damaged the electrical system, the heaters failed and the remaining fuel froze. Controllers thawed it as the craft neared the Sun, but could not get the main engine working, and abandoned the attempt to enter orbit five days before arrival.

missions.who: United Kingdom, carried by ESA's Mars Express
missions.for: Searching for signs of life in Martian soil, built on a small budget by a team led by Colin Pillinger.
missions.far: The surface. It was assumed for eleven years to have crashed.
missions.what: In January 2015 a NASA orbiter's camera found it sitting intact on Isidis Planitia, 5 km from its target. It had landed perfectly. Of its four solar panels, at least one had failed to fold open, which blocked the radio antenna underneath. It may have worked for months with no way of telling anyone. Pillinger had died eight months before it was found.
missions.primary: ESA/UK Commission of Inquiry, 2004; MRO HiRISE images released 16 January 2015

missions.for: Bringing 200 grams of the Martian moon Phobos back to Earth. It also carried Yinghuo-1, China's first Mars probe.
missions.far: A low parking orbit around Earth.
missions.what: The engines that should have sent it toward Mars never fired, probably because cheap, non-space-rated memory chips failed in the flight computer. It circled for two months, mostly silent, and fell into the Pacific on 15 January 2012.

missions.for: An X-ray observatory carrying a detector cooled to a twentieth of a degree above absolute zero, able to measure the motion of gas in galaxy clusters.
missions.far: Five weeks in orbit, and one landmark observation of the Perseus Cluster.
missions.what: Its attitude system wrongly decided the spacecraft was rotating and spun up a reaction wheel to correct it, which really did set it turning. When it tried to stop itself with thrusters, a set of incorrect values uploaded weeks earlier made the thrusters push the wrong way. It spun until its solar panels tore off. A replacement, XRISM, was launched in 2023.

missions.for: Proving Europe could land on Mars, ahead of a rover.
missions.far: Through the heat of entry and parachute deployment, to 3.7 km above the ground.
missions.what: The lander swung more than expected under its parachute, and a motion sensor maxed out for one second longer than the software allowed for. The computer calculated that its altitude was negative, concluded it had landed, released the parachute and shut down its thrusters after three seconds. It fell for 34 seconds and hit at 540 km/h.

missions.for: A 90-day search for signs of past water on Mars.
missions.far: Fourteen and a half years. It drove 45.16 km, farther than anything else has driven on another world, and found the water.
missions.what: A dust storm covered the whole planet in June 2018 and blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed. Its last message was a routine status report on 10 June. Engineers sent more than a thousand commands over the next eight months and heard nothing back. The mission was declared over on 13 February 2019.

missions.for: The first privately funded Moon landing, and Israel's first. Its name is the first word of Genesis: 'in the beginning'.
missions.far: Lunar orbit, then most of the way down.
missions.what: A motion sensor failed during the descent. The command sent to restart it reset the computer, which shut off the main engine. By the time the engine relit the lander was too low and too fast. It hit the Sea of Serenity at about 500 km/h, having sent back a last photograph from 22 km up.

missions.for: India's first Moon landing, near the south pole, with a small rover called Pragyan.
missions.far: 2.1 km above the surface.
missions.what: The engines slowed the lander harder than planned during braking, and the software was not permitted to correct fast enough to recover. It struck the surface about 500 metres from its target. The orbiter it came with is still working. Four years later Chandrayaan-3 landed a rebuilt Vikram in the same region, the first landing near the lunar south pole.

missions.for: For 53 years the largest single telescope on Earth: a 305-metre dish set in a sinkhole in Puerto Rico.
missions.far: Fifty-seven years of work. It found the first binary pulsar and the first planets outside the Solar System, measured Mercury's rotation and sent humanity's first deliberate message to the stars.
missions.what: A support cable pulled out of its socket in August 2020 and a second snapped in November. The telescope was declared too dangerous to repair. Twelve days later the remaining cables gave way, and the 900-tonne instrument platform fell 140 metres into the dish.
missions.primary: National Academies report on the Arecibo collapse, 2024

missions.for: China's first Mars rover, landed on its first attempt in May 2021 for a three-month mission.
missions.far: A year, and 1,921 metres across Utopia Planitia.
missions.what: It was put into hibernation to wait out the Martian winter and a season of dust storms, and was expected to wake by itself that December. It never did. Orbiter images showed it had not moved; dust on its solar panels is the likely reason.

missions.for: The first commercial Moon landing, carrying the United Arab Emirates' Rashid rover.
missions.far: Five kilometres above the surface.
missions.what: As the lander crossed the rim of a crater the ground dropped away by about 3 km. The software judged so large a jump in its altitude reading to be a sensor fault and ignored the sensor from then on. It descended slowly to what it believed was the surface, hovered at 5 km until its fuel ran out, and fell. A second ispace lander, Resilience, crashed in June 2025 after its laser rangefinder was slow to lock on.

missions.for: Russia's return to the Moon after 47 years, aimed at the south pole.
missions.far: Lunar orbit.
missions.what: An engine burn to lower the orbit should have lasted 84 seconds. The control unit failed to shut the engine off and it ran for 127. The lander's orbit now intersected the Moon. It left a fresh crater about 10 metres across.

missions.for: The first American Moon lander since Apollo 17, carrying twenty payloads.
missions.far: The Moon's distance, but not the Moon.
missions.what: Hours after launch a valve between the helium and oxidiser tanks failed to close again. Pressure built until the oxidiser tank ruptured. With its propellant leaking away, the team flew it for ten days, switched on every payload they could, and steered it back to burn up over the South Pacific.

missions.for: Five test flights to prove powered flight is possible in air 1% as thick as Earth's.
missions.far: Seventy-two flights over nearly three years, 17 km in all.
missions.what: On its last flight it came down over smooth, featureless sand, which gave its navigation camera nothing to track. It landed hard and at least one rotor blade broke. It still sits in Jezero crater, and still gathers weather data it has no way to send.
missions.primary: NASA announcement, 25 January 2024; JPL investigation, December 2024

missions.for: Drilling for ice near the lunar south pole.
missions.far: The surface, about 250 metres from its target, the most southerly landing yet made.
missions.what: Its altimeter gave poor readings in the long shadows near the pole. It came down in a small crater and fell on its side, with its solar panels pointing the wrong way. The batteries ran out the next day.

missions.for: Mapping where the Moon's water is, and in what form.
missions.far: One day.
missions.what: The small satellite separated from its rocket on 26 February 2025 and made contact. The next day it went quiet. Tracking suggested it was tumbling slowly with its solar panels turned away from the Sun. Teams listened for five months in case the panels drifted back into sunlight.

missions.for: Returning astronauts to the Moon by 2020, then going on to Mars.
missions.far: Five years, about nine billion dollars and one test flight of a prototype rocket.
missions.what: An independent review in 2009 found that the programme could not meet its goals on the money it was being given. It was cancelled in the 2011 budget. Its crew capsule, Orion, survived, and in April 2026 carried four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II.
missions.primary: Review of U.S. Human Spaceflight Plans Committee (Augustine), 2009; NASA Authorization Act of 2010

missions.for: Bringing to Earth the rock cores that the Perseverance rover has been collecting since 2021, chosen because they could hold evidence of ancient life.
missions.far: The samples are collected. About thirty sealed tubes are on Mars, some laid out on the ground at a depot and the rest inside the rover.
missions.what: A 2023 review put the cost at 8 to 11 billion dollars with samples arriving no earlier than 2040. NASA called the plan unworkable and asked for cheaper designs. In January 2026 Congress passed a budget that did not fund the programme. The tubes are built to last decades. China plans its own sample return, Tianwen-3, for around 2030.
missions.primary: MSR Independent Review Board report, September 2023; US fiscal year 2026 appropriations, January 2026
